entities.summary:
Andronikos of Rhodes was a Greek philosopher from Rhodes who served as the scholarch of the Peripatetic school from 305 BCE until his death in 60 BCE. He is best known for publishing a new edition of the works of Aristotle that forms the basis of the texts that survive today. This new edition, which Andronikos edited and revised, is considered one of the most important works of the Hellenistic period and had a profound impact on the development of Western philosophy.

Andronikos' work on the Aristotle's works was not without controversy. His edition was heavily influenced by the Stoic philosopher Zeno of Citium, who had become a prominent figure in the Peripatetic school during Andronikos' lifetime. This has led some scholars to question the accuracy of Andronikos' transmission of Aristotle's ideas, with some arguing that the Stoic influence has led to a loss of the original Aristotelian thought.

Despite these criticisms, Andronikos' edition of Aristotle's works remains the most authoritative and widely accepted version of the philosopher's writings. It is estimated that Andronikos' work on the Aristotle's works took over 50 years to complete, and it is likely that his edition was the result of a combination of his own scholarly research and the input of his fellow scholars.

Andronikos' legacy extends beyond his work on Aristotle's works. He is also remembered for his role in the development of the Stoic school, which would go on to play a significant role in the history of Western philosophy.

In conclusion, Andronikos of Rhodes was a significant figure in the history of Western philosophy, and his work on Aristotle's works had a profound impact on the development of the subject. Despite some controversy surrounding his transmission of Aristotle's ideas, Andronikos' edition remains the most authoritative and widely accepted version of the philosopher's writings.
